rounds.proof_sketch: For fixed input shape [128,1], size=128. block_size=256. Original: num_blocks=(128+256-1)/256=383/256=1. Mutated: num_blocks=(128+256+1)/256=385/256=1. Both integer divisions yield 1, so the mutation has no effect on num_blocks for this fixed size.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the ceiling-division formula from (size + block_size - 1) to (size + block_size + 1). However, for the fixed input shape of [128, 1], the flattened size is always 128. With block_size=256, the original formula computes (128+256-1)/256 = 383/256 = 1 block, while the mutated formula computes (128+256+1)/256 = 385/256 = 1 block. Since integer division truncates and both results equal 1, the number of allocated blocks is identical. Consequently, the kernel launch configuration, memory allocation, and computation all remain unchanged, producing bitwise-identical results regardless of input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The mutation only affects the num_blocks calculation, which evaluates to the same value (1) for size=128 and block_size=256. To kill this mutant would require changing the input size to a value where the formula difference matters (e.g., size=255 would give original: ceil(255/256)=1 vs mutated: (255+256+1)/256=2), but shape changes are prohibited.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing frameworks should include shape-variant testing for CUDA launch-parameter calculations, since many such mutations are only observable at specific size boundaries (e.g., multiples of block_size). For fixed-shape contracts, consider adding static analysis to detect when launch-parameter mutations are unreachable.
